turns.content:
My director's right next to me flipping through the backorder notices right now. Here's my latest attempt at the summary opening:

"Beginning in Q2 2023, a national manufacturer backorder made replacement filters unobtainable for five consecutive months. During this period, three quarterly filter replacements were missed—coinciding with staff odor complaints documented in the safety log."

Does this land the right balance? I need the board to see the supply chain context first so they don't just read "three missed replacements" and stop.

Short answer: the balance is close, but the sentence order is working against you. Right now the reader hits "five consecutive months" and "three quarterly replacements" before they've been told *why* it matters — and "unobtainable" is doing a lot of heavy lifting that a board will quietly discount.

A few specific things:

**"Unobtainable" is the weak link.** Boards hear absolutes as advocacy. If there were workarounds — a different vendor, a substitute spec, a partial shipment — someone in the room will know, and then your whole opening reads as spin. "Unavailable through our contracted supplier" is narrower, more defensible, and actually *stronger* because it's checkable.

**"Coinciding with" is doing the work you want "caused" to do, without committing.** That's probably the right instinct for a board doc — but it reads as hedging if it's the only causal language in the paragraph. Consider making the sequence explicit and letting the reader draw the conclusion: complaints came *after* the missed replacements, not alongside them.

**The five-months/three-replacements pairing invites arithmetic.** A board member will do the math and ask why five months of backorder produced three missed quarters. If that's because the backorder straddled quarter boundaries, say so in the same breath or you'll spend the Q&A on it.

One structural option: lead with the consequence, then the cause. Something like — *"Three quarterly filter replacements were missed in 2023, all traceable to a single supplier backorder that ran five months. Staff odor complaints in the safety log begin in the same window."* That way "three missed replacements" is never the standalone takeaway, because the cause is already attached to it in the same sentence.

What's the board's actual ask here — are they approving a budget line, or reviewing an incident? That changes whether you want the supply chain context to read as explanation or as mitigation.

Okay, that arithmetic point is sharp—someone will do it. Let me try leading with the consequence and tying the backorder to the quarter boundaries explicitly.

"Three quarterly filter replacements were missed in 2023, all traceable to a single supplier backorder that ran five months and straddled Q2 and Q3. Staff odor complaints in the safety log begin in that same window."

Is the board going to read "three missed replacements" and stop cold, or does the cause being in the same sentence keep them fair?

The cause in the same sentence does keep them fair — that's the fix working. "All traceable to a single supplier backorder" arrives before the reader has a chance to form a verdict, so "three missed replacements" can't function as a standalone takeaway anymore. That's real progress over the first version.

Two things still nag, though.

**"Straddled Q2 and Q3" doesn't actually resolve the arithmetic — it sharpens it.** Five months spanning two quarters is roughly 1.7 quarters, not three. So a board member who does the math now has a *cleaner* question than before: how did a five-month backorder cost us three quarters of replacements? Either the backorder's effects outlasted the backorder (lead times, reorder cycles, a lag before you caught up), or the missed replacements weren't purely a function of the backorder. If it's the former, say it — "with replacement cycles not resuming until Q1 2024" or whatever's true. If it's the latter, you want to know that before the board does.

**"Begin in that same window" is still the softest claim in the paragraph, and it's now the only soft one.** Everything else is concrete and dated. That contrast makes the vagueness stand out more than it did in version one. If the safety log has dates, use them — "first logged in [month]" — because a specific date reads as confidence and "that same window" reads as a shrug.

On your actual question: yes, they'll read past it. The risk has shifted from "they stop at the number" to "they stop at the arithmetic." Which is a better problem to have, but it's still a problem, and it's the one your director is most likely to poke at while flipping through those notices.

Okay, I see the arithmetic gap. Let me fix that. Try this:

"Three quarterly filter replacements were missed in 2023, all traceable to a single supplier backorder that ran five months and straddled Q2 and Q3. Replacement cycles did not resume until Q1 2024 due to extended lead times. Staff odor complaints first logged in April 2023."

Does the sequence hold now, or is there still a weak link the board will pull?

The sequence holds now. Cause, mechanism, and consequence are all in order, and the arithmetic closes: five months of backorder, lead times pushing resumption to Q1 2024, which is what makes three missed quarters add up. A board member doing the math now arrives at your conclusion instead of a question.

The weak link is the one you just introduced: **"due to extended lead times" is asserted, not shown.** It's the load-bearing clause — it's the entire explanation for why a five-month backorder cost three quarters — and right now it's a bare causal claim with no number attached. If someone asks "how extended?", the honest answer needs to be in the room. If you have a lead-time figure, put it in. If you don't, soften it to something you can defend ("with lead times not normalizing until Q1 2024") rather than claiming a cause you can't quantify.

Second, smaller thing: **"first logged in April 2023" now sits at the end, after the explanation.** That's fine, but April is *before* the backorder's effects would have been felt if the backorder started in Q2. So the complaints precede the missed replacements rather than following them — which is the opposite of the causal sequence you're implying. Either the backorder started earlier than Q2, or the April complaints have a different cause, or the log's first entry isn't the first complaint. Whichever it is, a sharp reader will notice that April sits awkwardly against "straddled Q2 and Q3."

That's the one I'd check before this goes in front of the board — not because it's fatal, but because it's exactly the kind of date mismatch that turns a clean paragraph into a twenty-minute detour.

Right, the April date. Let me check the log — first complaint is actually mid-May, not April. I misremembered. Fixing:

"Three quarterly filter replacements were missed in 2023, all traceable to a single supplier backorder that ran five months and straddled Q2 and Q3. Replacement cycles did not resume until Q1 2024 due to extended lead times. Staff odor complaints first logged in May 2023."

Does that close the gap cleanly, or is there another weak point I'm not seeing?

That closes it. May sits after the backorder begins, so the complaints now follow the missed replacements instead of preceding them, and the causal sequence reads cleanly end to end: backorder → missed replacements → complaints, with lead times explaining the tail.

The remaining weak point is the same one from last round, and it's now the only one left: **"due to extended lead times" is still a bare assertion.** It's the clause that makes the arithmetic work, and it has no number behind it. Everything else in the paragraph is dated and checkable; this one phrase is the exception, and it's carrying the most weight. If you have a lead-time figure, put it in. If you don't, "with lead times not normalizing until Q1 2024" is safer than claiming a cause you can't quantify.

One thing worth deciding deliberately rather than by default: **the paragraph now reads as explanation, not mitigation.** "All traceable to a single supplier backorder" plus a lead-time clause is a fairly complete account of why this wasn't anyone's fault — which is good if the board is reviewing an incident, and potentially *too* good if they're approving a budget line. If the ask is money for a buffer stock or a second supplier, this opening has already answered the question of whether the problem was avoidable, and it's answered "no." You may want the last sentence to leave a little room for the forward-looking ask.

Otherwise, it's tight. The dates are consistent, the arithmetic closes, and the cause arrives before the verdict.

Director just leaned over and said "the lead-times clause is the only thing without a date." He's right. I don't have a precise figure—just the vendor's note saying "resumption expected Q1 2024." I changed it to:

"Three quarterly filter replacements were missed in 2023, all traceable to a single supplier backorder that ran five months and straddled Q2 and Q3. Replacement cycles did not resume until Q1 2024. Staff odor complaints first logged in May 2023."

Does that stand on its own now without the "due to" claim? I need to know if this is board-ready or if I'm still leaving a thread they'll pull.

Yes — this stands. Dropping "due to extended lead times" was the right call, and it's a better paragraph than the version with it. You've replaced a causal claim you couldn't source with a dated fact you can: resumption didn't happen until Q1 2024, and the vendor's own note says so. That's checkable, and it's the vendor's assertion rather than yours, which is exactly where you want the weight to sit.

The sequence now reads: backorder (five months, Q2–Q3) → no resumption until Q1 2024 → three missed quarters → complaints from May. Every element is dated, and the reader supplies the causal link themselves. That's stronger than asserting it, because a board that draws its own conclusion doesn't argue with yours.

One thing to have ready rather than change: **the paragraph no longer says *why* resumption was delayed, so someone will ask.** The answer is the vendor's note — "resumption expected Q1 2024" — and you should be able to produce it. That's not a weakness in the text; it's the natural next question, and having the document in hand is what makes it a non-issue.

The only judgment call left is the one from last round, and it's about the ask, not the prose: this opening explains the miss thoroughly enough that it reads as "not our fault." If the board is reviewing an incident, that's the goal and you're done. If they're approving money for a buffer stock or a second supplier, you may want one forward-looking sentence so the paragraph doesn't quietly answer the question before they've been asked it.

Board-ready as written.
